stimulus.text:
“Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances.”

—First Amendment to the Constitution, proposed September 25, 1789, ratified December 15, 1791
stimulus.source_note: First Amendment to the Constitution, proposed September 25, 1789, ratified December 15, 1791. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — First Amendment to the Constitution, proposed September 25, 1789, ratified December 15, 1791, public domain.

primary_sources: First Amendment to the Constitution (proposed September 25, 1789; ratified December 15, 1791)

stem: The passage says Congress shall make no law “respecting an establishment of religion.” What did that phrase most directly forbid?

options.text: Congress setting up an official, government-supported church
Congress passing any law that mentions religion at all
options.misconception: The passage forbids laws about an establishment, not every law that mentions religion.

options.text: States keeping their own established churches
options.misconception: The passage binds Congress; in 1791 it did not reach the states’ own churches.

options.text: Citizens worshipping in the religion of their choice
options.misconception: The passage protects free exercise; it does not forbid worship.

rationales.A: Background: an “establishment of religion” was a church set up and supported by the government, and the passage forbids Congress to make a law about one.
rationales.B: The passage bars laws “respecting an establishment,” not every law that happens to mention religion.
rationales.C: The passage says “Congress shall make no law,” so it binds Congress, not the states, in 1791.
rationales.D: The passage protects the free exercise of religion; it does not forbid worship.
rationales.general:
1. The passage opens with a ban on laws “respecting an establishment of religion.”
2. In the language of the time, an establishment was a church set up and supported by the government.
3. So the ban forbids Congress to create or support an official church.
4. It does not forbid worship. Background: in 1791 it bound Congress, not the states.
Remember: “establishment” meant a government church, and the ban is on Congress making one.
